en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-āsrava-vibhaṅga-sūtra*, from the *Madhyama Āgama*, translated by the Tripitaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han dynasty during the reign of Emperor Ling.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kuru at a place for practicing healing called Dharma. At that time,
When the people of Kōshala were assembled,
the Buddha addressed them: “O bhikṣus!”
The bhikṣus replied, “So be it. The bhikṣus heard it from the Buddha.
The Buddha then addressed them thus:
"Bhikṣus, listen.

I shall preach the Dharma for you, which is beneficial in its beginning, beneficial in its middle, and beneficial in its conclusion; it is meaningful, possesses the proper method, and fully manifests the practice of the mind."
"You should listen attentively, receive it with care, and bear it in mind as you hear it.
The bhikṣu replied, "So be it."
The bhikṣu then heard it from the Buddha and spoke thus: “Bhikṣus!...”

One should know the outflows; one should also know the origin from which the outflows arise; one should also know the calamity received because of the outflows; one should also know the distribution of the outflows; one should also know the exhaustion of the outflows; and one should also know what practice must be undertaken to bring the outflows to an end.

“Monks! You should know feeling; you should also know the origin of feeling; you should also know how suffering arises from feeling; you should also know the distribution of feeling; you should also know the cessation of feeling; and you should also know what practice one must undertake to bring feeling to an end.”

“Monks! You should know perception; you should know the origin of perception; you should know how suffering arises from perception; you should know the diversity of perception; you should know the cessation of perception; and you should know what practice leads to the ending of perception.”

“Bhikṣus! You should know sensual desire; you should know the origin of sensual desire; you should know the calamity resulting from sensual desire; you should know the distribution of sensual desire; you should know the exhaustion of sensual desire; and you should know what practice must be undertaken to bring sensual desire to an end.”

“Monks! You should know volitional formations; you should know the origin of volitional formations; you should know the suffering that arises from volitional formations; you should know the distribution of volitional formations; you should know the cessation of volitional formations; and you should know what kind of practice must be undertaken to bring volitional formations to an end.”

“Monks! You should know suffering; you should also know the origin of suffering; you should also know the affliction that arises from suffering; you should also know the distribution of suffering; you should also know the cessation of suffering; and you should also know what practice must be undertaken to bring suffering to an end.”

“Monks! You should know the taints; you should know the origin of the taints; you should know the calamity resulting from the taints; you should know the distribution of the taints; you should know the cessation of the taints; and you should know what practice one must undertake to bring the taints to an end.”
"What are the outflows that should be known? There are three outflows:
first, the outflow of sensual desire; second, the outflow of existence; and third, the outflow of ignorance."
This is how one knows the outflows.
What is meant by "knowing that the outflows have existed from the beginning"?
It means that ignorance is the root of the outflows; they have existed from this root.
In this way, one knows that outflows (āsrava) exist from the very beginning.
What is it to know that one receives retribution from outflows?

It means that from the outflows of deluded conduct, one acts according to those outflows and receives retribution according to those actions, whether falling into a favorable state or a wretched state.
In this way, one understands that from outflows (*āsrava*) comes the reaping of calamity.
What is meant by "knowing the distribution of the outflows"?

It means that falling into hell is a distinct course of action; falling into the animal realm is a distinct course of action; falling into the realm of hungry ghosts is a distinct course of action; falling into the heavenly realms is a distinct course of action; and falling among humans is a distinct course of action.
This is how one knows the distribution of the outflows (*āsrava*).
What is that which should be known as the exhaustion of the outflows?
It is said: when delusion (*moha*) is exhausted, the outflows are then exhausted; as it is, they are exhausted.
In this way, one knows the exhaustion of the outflows.

What is it that should be known and practiced so as to bring the outflows to an end? It is the practice of the Eightfold Path: [1] Right View, [2] Right Intention, [3] Right Speech, [4] Right Action, [5] Right Livelihood, [6] Right Effort, [7] Right Mindfulness, and [8] Right Concentration.

First is right view, second is right intention, third is right speech, fourth is right action, fifth is right livelihood, sixth is right effort, seventh is right mindfulness, and eighth is right concentration;
thus one knows how to practice so as to bring an end to the outflows.

"Monks! If a monk knows the outflows (āsrava) as they are; knows how the outflows have existed from the beginning as it is; knows how one incurs calamity from the outflows as it is; knows the distribution of the outflows as it is; knows the exhaustion of the outflows as it is; and knows the practice for bringing the outflows to an end as it is—this is called a monk who is weary of and disgusted with the world, who practices purity, and who has attained the Path so that the outflows are brought to their final end."

“Monks! You should know feeling; you should know the origin of feeling; you should know the suffering that results from feeling; you should know the distribution of feeling; you should know the cessation of feeling; and you should know what practice must be undertaken to bring feeling to an end.”
"What is that which should be known as feeling?
It is said that there are three feelings:
first, pleasant feeling; second, painful feeling; and third, neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling."
This is how one understands suffering.
What is meant by "one should understand that suffering has its origin"?
It refers to fundamental volition and aspiration.
In this way, one knows that suffering has existed from the very beginning.
What is meant by "knowing that one incurs calamity from suffering"?
It refers to whatever one thinks about; this, moreover, is suffering.
In this way, one knows that suffering brings about retribution.
What is meant by "knowing the distribution of suffering"?
It is thus, bhikṣus!
A bhikṣu experiences a pleasant feeling and knows it as a pleasant feeling;
he experiences a painful feeling and knows it as a painful feeling;
he experiences a neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling and knows it as a neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling.
One experiences a pleasant bodily contact and knows that one experiences a pleasant bodily contact;
one experiences an unpleasant bodily contact and knows that one experiences an unpleasant bodily contact;
one experiences a neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant bodily contact and knows that one experiences a neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant bodily contact.
Pleasant feeling as contact, one knows pleasant feeling as contact;
painful feeling as contact, one knows painful feeling as contact;
neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling as contact, one knows neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling as contact.
One knows the attainment of the expectation of pleasant feeling, and one knows the knowledge of the expectation of pleasant feeling;
one knows the attainment of the expectation of painful feeling, and one knows the knowledge of the expectation of painful feeling;
one knows the attainment of the expectation of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, and one knows the knowledge of the expectation of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
One does not expect to obtain pleasant feeling, nor does one seek to know pleasant feeling;
one does not expect to obtain painful feeling, nor does one seek to know painful feeling;
one does not expect to obtain neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, nor does one seek to know neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
When one dwells amidst pleasant sensations, one knows: "I dwell amidst pleasant sensations";
when one dwells amidst painful sensations, one knows: "I dwell amidst painful sensations";
when one dwells amidst sensations that are neither pleasant nor painful, one knows: "I dwell amidst sensations that are neither pleasant nor painful."
One dwells detached from pleasant feelings and knows that one dwells detached from pleasant feelings;
one dwells detached from painful feelings and knows that one dwells detached from painful feelings;
one dwells detached from neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings and knows that one dwells detached from neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.
This is how one knows the distribution of feeling.
What is meant by "knowing the exhaustion of feeling"?
It means that when mindfulness and reflection are withdrawn, feeling is then exhausted.
In this way, one knows the exhaustion of suffering.

What is the practice that should be undertaken to bring suffering to an end? It is the eightfold path: [the right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration].

First is right view, second is right intention, third is right speech, fourth is right action, fifth is right livelihood, sixth is right effort, seventh is right mindfulness, and eighth is right concentration;
thus one knows the practice of the factors of enlightenment so as to bring suffering to an end.

If a bhikṣu knows suffering as it is, knows how suffering originates as it is, knows how one incurs calamity from suffering as it is, knows the distribution of suffering as it is, knows the exhaustion of suffering as it is, and knows the practice for bringing suffering to its ultimate end as it is, he is called a bhikṣu who has become weary of and disgusted with the world, who practices purity, and who has attained the Path so that suffering is brought to its ultimate end.

“Monks! You should know perception; you should know the origin of perception; you should know how suffering arises from perception; you should know the diversity of perception; you should know the cessation of perception; and you should know what practice must be undertaken to bring perception to an end.”
“What is that which should be known as perception?
There are four types of perception:
first, limited perception; second, vast perception; third, immeasurable perception; and fourth, perception of nothingness.”
This is how one understands ideation.
What is meant by "understanding that ideation has existed from the beginning"?
It means that ideation is itself the beginning.
In this way, one understands that thought has existed from the very beginning.
What is meant by "knowing that one incurs calamity from thought"?
It means that as one thinks, so one acts; as one thinks, so one conducts oneself—this is called volitional formation (*saṃskāra*).
In this way, one understands that suffering arises from mental volition (*saṃskāra*).
What is meant by "knowing the distribution of mental volitions"?

It means that the mental volition regarding forms is distinct, the mental volition regarding sounds is distinct, the mental volition regarding odors is distinct, the mental volition regarding tastes is distinct, and the mental volition regarding the coarse and subtle tactile sensations of the body is also distinct.
Thus is the knowledge of the distribution of perceptions.
What is the knowledge that perceptions should be brought to an end?
It means that when perceptions have already been exhausted, perceptions are then extinguished.
Thus is the knowledge that thoughts have been exhausted.

What is the practice that should be undertaken to bring thoughts to their end? It is the eightfold path: [the right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration].

First is right view, second is right intention, third is right speech, fourth is right action, fifth is right livelihood, sixth is right effort, seventh is right mindfulness, and eighth is right concentration;
thus one knows how to practice so as to bring thought to its completion.

"Monks! When a monk knows thoughts as they are, knows how thoughts originate from their root, knows how misfortune is incurred through thoughts, knows the distribution of thoughts, knows the exhaustion of thoughts, and knows the practice by which thoughts are brought to an end—this is called a monk who has become weary of and disgusted with the world, who practices purity, and who attains the Path so that thoughts are exhausted and brought to an end."

“Monks! You should know sensual desire; you should know the origin of sensual desire; you should know the suffering that arises from sensual desire; you should know the pervasion of sensual desire; you should know the cessation of sensual desire; and you should know the practice by which sensual desire is brought to an end.”
"What is that which should be known as sensual desire?

It refers to the five kinds of sensual desires: the desire for acquisition, the desire most present in the mind, and the proximity of forms that are lovely and can be craved according to one's wishes."

What are the five? First, there is the desire for forms cognizable by the eye: the attainment of desire, the preeminent desire within the mind, the craving for form, the inclination toward it according to one's will, and the proximity of greed;

second, there is the desire for sounds cognizable by the ear: the attainment of desire, the preeminent desire within the mind, the craving for sound, the inclination toward it according to one's will, and the proximity of greed.

Third is the desire for odors to be perceived by the nose: the attainment of desire, the preeminent desire in the mind, the affection for forms, and the proximity of what is agreeable and desirable according to one's will;

fourth is the desire for tastes to be perceived by the mouth: the attainment of desire, the preeminent desire in the mind, the affection for forms, and the proximity of what is agreeable and desirable according to one's will;

fifth is the desire for coarse and subtle tactile sensations to be known by the body: the attainment of desire, the preeminent desire in the mind, the affection for forms, and the proximity of what is agreeable and desirable according to one's will.
In this way, one understands sensual desire.
What is meant by "understanding that sensual desire exists from its origin"?
It means that its origin is volition.
In this way, one knows that sensual desire exists from its very origin.
What is it to know how one incurs calamity from sensual desire?

When one has become attached to what is desired, there arises longing, strife, and yearning; thus, as one harbors thoughts of calamity, one follows after that calamity, whether to a good destination or a bad one.
Thus one should understand that from sensual desire comes the reception of calamity.
"What is meant by knowing the distribution of sensual desire?

It is that the sensual desire for forms is distinct, the sensual desire for sounds is distinct, the sensual desire for odors is distinct, the sensual desire for tastes is distinct, and the sensual desire for tactile objects—whether coarse or subtle—is also distinct."
Thus is the knowledge of the distribution of craving.
What is the knowledge of the exhaustion of craving?
It is that when volitional formations are exhausted, craving is exhausted.
In this way, one knows the exhaustion of craving.
What is the practice that should be undertaken to bring craving to an end?
It is the practice of the Eightfold Path:

First is right view, second is right intention, third is right speech, fourth is right action, fifth is right livelihood, sixth is right effort, seventh is right mindfulness, and eighth is right concentration;
thus, by knowing and practicing these, one brings an end to craving and desire.
"O bhikṣus! If one knows that sensual desire is thus;

knows that sensual desire originates from such a root; knows that the retribution received from sensual desire is thus; knows the distribution of sensual desire is thus; knows the exhaustion of sensual desire is thus; and knows how to practice so as to bring sensual desire to its ultimate end—this is called a bhikṣu who is weary of and disgusted with the world, who practices purity, and who attains the Path so that sensual desire is completely exhausted."

“Monks! You should know volitional formations; you should know the origin of volitional formations; you should know how suffering and merit arise from volitional formations; you should know the diversity of volitional formations; you should know the cessation of volitional formations; and you should know what kind of practice leads to the ending of volitional formations.”
"What is meant by 'knowing formations' (*saṃskāra*)?
That which is directed toward and not separated from what one contemplates is 'formation';
such is knowing formations."
"What is meant by knowing that action arises from its origin?
It means that conditioned by craving there is becoming, and conditioned by craving there is the origin of action;
this is what is meant by knowing that action arises from its origin."
"What is meant by knowing that one receives calamity or fortune according to one's conduct?
It means that there are dark deeds which bring dark calamities, causing one to fall into the lower realms;
there are pure and white deeds which bring pure and white fortune, enabling one to attain the highest states."
This is what is meant by knowing that one receives calamity or fortune according to one's actions.
What is meant by "knowing the distribution of actions"?
It refers to dark actions, from which one receives dark calamity;
There are actions that are pure and white, which result in pure and white blessings;
there are actions that are black and white, which lead to black and white calamities and blessings;
and there are actions that are neither black nor white, which result in blessings from them.
When all formations have been completely exhausted, this is what is meant by knowing the distribution of formations.
What is meant by "knowing the exhaustion of formations"?
It means that when craving is exhausted, formations are thereby exhausted.
In this way, one knows the exhaustion of formations.
What is meant by "knowing how to practice so as to bring the practice to its completion"?
It refers to the eightfold noble path:

First is right view, second is right intention, third is right speech, fourth is right action, fifth is right livelihood, sixth is right effort, seventh is right mindfulness, and eighth is right concentration;
thus one knows how to practice and brings the practice to completion.

"O monks! If a monk knows conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) as they are; knows how conditioned formations originate from their root as it is; knows how one incurs calamity through conditioned formations as it is; knows the distribution of conditioned formations as it is; knows the cessation of conditioned formations as it is; and knows how to undergo and bring conditioned formations to completion as it is—this is called a monk who is weary of and disgusted with the world, whose conduct is pure, who has attained the Path, and who has brought conditioned formations to their final end."

“Monks! You should know suffering; you should also know the origin of suffering; you should also know the retribution that arises from suffering; you should also know the distribution of suffering; you should also know the cessation of suffering; and you should also know what practice must be undertaken to bring suffering to an end.”
"What is meant by 'one should know suffering'?

It means one should know that birth is suffering; one should know that old age is suffering; one should know that illness is suffering; one should know that death is suffering; one should know that being near those one does not like is suffering; one should know that separation from what one loves is suffering; one should know that not obtaining what one seeks is suffering; and one should know that, in brief, the five aggregates are suffering. This is what is meant by knowing suffering."
"What is meant by knowing that suffering has its origin in the fundamental?
It means that the fundamental is ignorance (*moha*); ignorance is the root of suffering;
such is the way of knowing that suffering has its origin in the fundamental."
"What is it that one should know as resulting in calamity from painful feeling?

It refers to those who are deluded, who have not heard the sutras, and who are worldly people; when they experience intense suffering within their own bodies—extreme pain, the most agonizing sensation that is disagreeable—they should contemplate the severance of this [suffering] from its source."

Seeking from the outside means being mindful of external conditioned phenomena; relying on the outside for one's seeking, there may be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, using one word, two words, three words, four words, five words, or a hundred words, maintain incantations and perform sacrifices, claiming that through these one can attain liberation from bodily suffering. Thus they seek out suffering or the calamity of suffering;
in this way, they understand that calamity arises from the sensation of suffering.
"What is meant by 'knowing the distribution of suffering'?

It means that there is suffering that is slight but its retribution is long-lasting; or suffering that is slight but its retribution is quickly resolved; or suffering that is great but its retribution is long-lasting; or suffering that is great but its retribution is quickly resolved.
This is what is meant by knowing the distribution of suffering."
"What is meant by 'knowing the exhaustion of suffering'?
It means that when delusion has been exhausted, suffering is exhausted;
this is what is meant by knowing the exhaustion of suffering."
“What is that which, when practiced and undertaken, should be known as leading to the end of suffering? It is the Eightfold Path:
first, right view; second, right intention; third, right speech; fourth, right action; fifth, right livelihood; sixth, right effort; seventh, right mindfulness; eighth, right concentration.”
In this way, one knows the practice that brings an end to suffering.

Monks, when a monk thus knows suffering as it is, knows how suffering originates as it is, knows how the retribution of suffering arises as it is, knows the distribution of suffering as it is, knows the cessation of suffering as it is, and knows the practice that brings an end to suffering as it is— this is called a monk who is weary of and disgusted with the world, who practices purity, and who has attained the Path so that suffering is brought to its final end.
Thus spoke the Buddha.

The bhikṣus received and took to heart what the Buddha had taught; they practiced that which the Buddha taught with joy, and through such practice, they attained purity and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This concludes the *Āsravavibhaṅga Sūtra* as spoken by the Buddha.
